Much of the existing transmission and distribution infrastructure contains legacy components that were designed for unidirectional power flow and simpler operating conditions, often installed 30-50 years ago when grid requirements were fundamentally different. Rural and remote areas may have particularly outdated infrastructure due to lower investment priorities, while urban areas face the challenge of upgrading aging systems without service interruptions to dense populations (McKenna et al. 2025). • Transformersrepresent some of the longest-lasting assets in the grid, with some units operating for 40-50 years or more. Legacy transformers lack monitoring capabilities that provide real-time information about load- ing, temperature, and condition. Without this observability, utilities must rely on periodic manual inspections and conservative operating practices, potentially underutilizing capacity or missing early warning signs of equipment failure. • Transmission Linesand associated infrastructure were designed for traditional grid operations and may require upgrades to support new transmission patterns, increased loading from renewable integration, or enhanced monitoring capabilities for better situational awareness. 8 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications • Voltage Regulatorsin legacy systems often operate independently with limited coordination capabilities. Modern grid operations require more sophisticated voltage control that can coordinate across multiple devices and respond to rapidly changing conditions from distributed generation and dynamic loads. The challenge of modernizing decades-old transmission and distribution infrastructure is compounded by its es- sential role: upgrades must enhance capabilities without compromising the continuous, reliable service that users depend on daily. 2.2.3 Protection and Grid Management Systems Grid protection and control systems ensure safe and reliable operation, but legacy versions often lack the speed, coordination, and communication capabilities needed for modern grid operations. • Protection Devicesinclude relays, circuit breakers, and other equipment designed to isolate faults and protect grid infrastructure. Legacy protection systems often operate with fixed settings and limited coordination capa- bilities. They may not be able to adapt to bidirectional power flows, rapid changes from renewable resources, or the need for more selective protection schemes that minimize outage impacts. • Programmable Logic Controllers (PLC) and Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) Con- trolsform the communication and control backbone of grid operations. Legacy systems often use proprietary protocols, have limited cybersecurity features, and may not support the real-time communication needed for advanced grid applications. The integration of distributed resources and the need for faster grid response times challenge these older control systems. • Electrical Sensors and Phasor Measurement Units (PMU)provide critical grid monitoring capabilities. Legacy sensors may lack the precision, communication capabilities, or real-time data provision needed for advanced grid applications like wide-area monitoring and control. The shift from unidirectional, centralized power flows to bidirectional, distributed generation fundamentally changes grid dynamics, making the upgrade of these protection and control systems essential for safe, reliable operations rather than optional improvements. 2.2.4 Load Management and Power Quality Equipment Equipment designed to manage power quality and loads often requires upgrades to support bidirectional power flows
